<!-- question-1: body_md -->
\label{Q:TheQuestion}
Given two $q$-commuting isometric pairs $(V_1,V_2)$ and $(V_1',V_2')$, when are the associated $C^*$-algebras $C^*(V_1,V_2)$ and $C^*(V_1',V_2')$ unitarily equivalent?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{T:q-BCL}
If $(V_1,V_2)$ is a pure pair (see \eqref{pure} for the definition) of $q$-commuting isometries on ${\mathcal H}$, then there exist a Hilbert space ${\mathcal F}$, a projection $P\in{\mathcal B}({\mathcal F})$, and a unitary $U\in{\mathcal B}({\mathcal F})$ such that $(V_1,V_2)$ is unitarily equivalent to
\begin{align}\label{isomod1}
\Bigl(
T_z R_q \otimes UP + R_q\otimes UP^\perp,
\quad
R_{\overline{q}}T_z \otimes P^\perp U^* + R_{\overline{q}}\otimes PU^*
\Bigr)
\quad \text{on} \quad H^2\otimes {\mathcal F}.
\end{align}

The triple $({\mathcal F},P,U)$ is uniquely determined up to unitary equivalence, i.e., if $(V_1,V_2)$ and $(V_1',V_2')$ are pairs of $q$-commuting isometries on ${\mathcal H}$ and ${\mathcal H}'$, with associated triple $({\mathcal F},P,U)$ and $({\mathcal F}',P',U')$, then $(V_1,V_2)$ and $(V_1',V_2')$ are jointly unitarily equivalent if and only if there exists a unitary  $\tau:{\mathcal F}\to {\mathcal F}'$ such that $\tau(P,U)=(P',U')\tau$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{T:CPcross}
Let ${\mathcal A}$ be a $C^*$-algebra and ${\mathcal I}\subseteq {\mathcal A}$ a closed two-sided $*$-ideal. If the quotient map $\pi:{\mathcal A}\to {\mathcal A}/{\mathcal I}$ admits a completely positive cross section $\rho$, then for any $C^*$-algebra ${\mathcal B}$, ${\mathcal I}\otimes {\mathcal B}$ is a closed two-sided ideal in ${\mathcal A}\otimes {\mathcal B}$ and the quotient algebra $({\mathcal A}\otimes {\mathcal B})/( {\mathcal I}\otimes {\mathcal B})$ is $*$-isomorphic to $({\mathcal A}/{\mathcal I})\otimes {\mathcal B}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{T:quotient} Let ${\mathcal A}$ and ${\mathcal B}$ be unital $C^*$-algebras faithfully represented on ${\mathcal H}$ and $\widetilde{{\mathcal H}}$, respectively, with ${\mathcal K}\subseteq {\mathcal A}$ and ${\mathcal K}\subseteq {\mathcal B}$ where ${\mathcal K}$ always denotes the ideal of compact operators on the relevant Hilbert space. Let $\pi:{\mathcal A}\to {\mathcal A}/{\mathcal K}$ and $\pi':{\mathcal B}\to {\mathcal B}/{\mathcal K}$ be the corresponding quotient maps, and assume that both $\pi$, $\pi'$ admit completely positive cross sections. Then $({\mathcal A}\otimes {\mathcal B})/{\mathcal K}$ is $*$-isomorphic to a closed $*$-subalgebra of $(({\mathcal A}/{\mathcal K})\otimes {\mathcal B})\oplus ({\mathcal A}\otimes ({\mathcal B}/{\mathcal K}))$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{L:block-unitary-index}
Let $W\in{\mathcal B}({\mathcal H})$ be unitary and let ${\mathcal M}\subset {\mathcal H}$ be a closed subspace. With respect to the orthogonal decomposition ${\mathcal H}={\mathcal M}\oplus{\mathcal M}^{\perp}$, write
$$
W=\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\ C&D\end{bmatrix}.
$$If $B\colon{\mathcal M}^{\perp}\to{\mathcal M}$ is compact, then $A$ and $D$ are semi-Fredholm and
$$
\operatorname{ind} A=-\operatorname{ind} D.
$$
Moreover, $A$ is Fredholm if and only if $C$ is also compact.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
From the $(1,1)$-entry of $WW^*=I$ we obtain $AA^*+BB^*=I_{{\mathcal M}}$. Since $BB^*$ is compact, the image of $A$ in the Calkin algebra ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal M})/{\mathcal K}$ is right-invertible; hence $A$ is (right) semi-Fredholm. Similarly, the $(2,2)$-entry of $W^*W=I$ gives $B^*B+D^*D=I_{{\mathcal M}^{\perp}}$, so $D$ is semi-Fredholm. We claim that the restriction $$
C\mid_{\ker A}\colon \ker A\to \ker D^*
$$ is unitary. 

To see that it is an isometry, let $x\in\ker A$. From the $(2,1)$-entry of $W^*W=I$ we have $B^*Ax+D^*Cx=0$, so $Cx\in\ker D^*$. From the $(1,1)$-entry of $W^*W=I$ we have $A^*Ax+C^*Cx=x$, hence $C^*Cx=x$.

For surjectivity, let $y\in\ker D^*$. The $(1,2)$-entry of $WW^*=I$ yields $AC^*y+BD^*y=0$, so $C^*y\in\ker A$. Using the $(2,2)$-entry of $WW^*=I$, namely $CC^*+DD^*=I_{{\mathcal M}^{\perp}}$, and $D^*y=0$, we obtain $CC^*y=y$.

Therefore $\dim\ker A=\dim\ker D^*$. A similar computation shows that the map $B^*\mid_{\ker A^*}\colon\ker A^*\to\ker D$ is unitary, so $\dim\ker A^*=\dim\ker D$. Consequently,
$$
\operatorname{ind} A=\dim\ker A-\dim\ker A^*=\dim\ker D^*-\dim\ker D=-\operatorname{ind} D.
$$
For the final assertion, first assume that $C$ is compact. Then the $(1,1)$-entry of $W^*W$ gives $A^*A+C^*C=I_{{\mathcal M}}$, so $A^*A-I_{{\mathcal M}}\in{\mathcal K}$ and hence $A$ is left semi-Fredholm. Together with the right semi-Fredholmness, this implies that $A$ is Fredholm. 

Conversely, assume that $A$ is Fredholm. Since $AA^*-I\in{\mathcal K}$, we have $\pi(A)^{-1}=\pi(A^*)$ in ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal M})/{\mathcal K}$. Therefore, $\pi(I-A^*A)=0$. Hence $C^*C=I-A^*A\in{\mathcal K}$, which implies that $C$ is compact.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{T:CommIdeal}
Consider the unitarily implemented embedding
$$
\iota:C^*(V_1,V_2)\to C^*(R_q,T_z)\otimes C^*(P,U)
$$
defined by
$
\iota: A\mapsto \tau_{\operatorname{BCL}}\cdot A\cdot \tau_{\operatorname{BCL}}^*
$
for every $A\in C^*(V_1,V_2)$. Then the image of the defect ideal ${\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$ under $\iota$ is 
$
{\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U).
$
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
By the definition of the unitary $\tau_{\rm BCL}$, we have
$$
\iota (V_1)=T_z R_q \otimes UP + R_q\otimes UP^\perp
\quad\mbox{and}\quad
\iota (V_2)=R_{\overline{q}}T_z \otimes  P^\perp U^*+R_{\overline{q}} \otimes PU^*.
$$
For later use, we list in Table \ref{tab:three-column} the images under $\iota$ of some important commutators that lie in the defect ideal ${\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$.

\begin{table}[ht!]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{l c}
\toprule
${\mathcal C}$ & $\iota({\mathcal C})$ \\
\midrule
$[V^*_1,V_1]$ & $\widetilde{P_0} \otimes UPU^*$ \\
$[V^*_2,V_2]$ & $\widetilde{P_0} \otimes P^\perp$ \\
\midrule
$V_2[V^*_1,V_1]V^*_2$ & $\widetilde{P_0} \otimes P$ \\
$V_1[V^*_2,V_2]+[V^*_1,V_1]V^*_2$ & $R_q\widetilde{P_0} \otimes U=\widetilde{P_0}\otimes U$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Commutators}
\label{tab:three-column}
\end{table}
The ideal ${\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U)$ contains the generators of $\iota({\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}})$, so
$\iota({\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}})\subseteq {\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U)$.

Since $ \widetilde{P_0}\otimes U$ and $\widetilde{P_0}\otimes P$ belong to $\iota ({\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}})$, it follows that $\widetilde{P_0}\otimes A\in \iota ({\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}})$ for any $A\in C^*(P,U)$. Moreover, because $\iota (V_1V_2)=T_z\otimes I\in \iota(C^*(V_1,V_2))$, we obtain for $n\geq 0$ that
$$
\widetilde{P_n}\otimes A = (T_z^n\otimes I)(\widetilde{P_0}\otimes A)(T_z^{*n}\otimes I)\in \iota({\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}).
$$
In particular, $\iota ({\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}})$ contains $F\otimes A$ for every rank-one operator $F$ and every $A\in C^*(P,U)$, and hence ${\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U)\subseteq \iota({\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}})$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\cite[Theorem 2]{MR2176158}\label{L:SEirrational}
For irrational $\theta$, the sequence 
$$
0 \to {\mathcal K} \xrightarrow{} {\mathcal T}({\mathcal A}_\theta) \xrightarrow{\pi} {\mathcal A}_{\theta} \to 0
$$
is short exact and admits the unital completely positive cross section $\sigma$, where $\pi$ is the canonical quotient map.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{L:SEtensored}
The sequence
$$
0 \to {\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U) \xrightarrow{} C^*(R_q,T_z)\otimes C^*(P,U) \xrightarrow{\pi\otimes 1} C^*(R_q,M_z)\otimes C^*(P,U) \to 0
$$
is exact.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since the short exact sequence in Lemma~\ref{L:SEirrational} admits a completely positive cross section, Theorem \ref{T:CPcross} (applied to $C^*(P,U)$) implies that ${\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U)$ is a closed two-sided $*$-ideal of $C^*(R_q,T_z)\otimes C^*(P,U)$ and that the quotient is canonically $*$-isomorphic to $(C^*(R_q,T_z)/{\mathcal K})\otimes C^*(P,U)$. This gives the desired exactness.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{L:Defect kernel}
The map $(\pi\otimes 1)\iota :C^*(V_1,V_2)\to C^*(R_q,M_z)\otimes C^*(P,U)$ is a $*$-homomorphism satisfying $\ker (\pi\otimes 1)\iota ={\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$ and $(\pi\otimes 1)\iota (V_j)=\widetilde{V}_j$ for $j=1,2$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
It is clear that $(\pi\otimes 1)\iota$ is a $*$-homomorphism. Moreover,
$$\ker(\pi\otimes1)\iota=\iota (C^*(V_1,V_2))\cap \ker (\pi\otimes1)=\iota (C^*(V_1,V_2))\cap \bigl({\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U)\bigr)={\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U),$$
where last equality follows from Theorem~\ref{T:CommIdeal}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
The map $\Psi$ is linear and contractive. Moreover, $\Psi(A)\in \iota (C^*(V_1,V_2))$ for every $A\in C^*(\widetilde{V}_1,\widetilde{V}_2)$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Linearity and contractivity of $\Psi$ are immediate. To see that $\Psi(A)\in \iota(C^*(V_1,V_2))$, it suffices to consider $*$-monomials $A=\widetilde{V_1}^{*n_1}\widetilde{V_2}^{*n_2}\widetilde{V_1}^{n_3}\widetilde{V_2}^{n_4}$, $n_i\geq 0 $. Since $\Psi(\widetilde{V_i})=\iota(V_i)$ and $\Psi(\widetilde{V_i}^*)=\iota(V_i^*)$ for $i=1,2$, we obatin
\begin{align*}\Psi(A)=(P_{H^2}\otimes I)\ensuremath{\left.A\right|_{H^2\otimes {\mathcal F}}}=\iota (V_1^{*n_1}V_2^{*n_2}V_1^{n_3}V_2^{n_4})
\end{align*} using the properties of the unitary extension.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{T:Generalized Toeplitz} Define $s: C^*(\widetilde{V}_1,\widetilde{V}_2)\to C^*(V_1,V_2)$ by 
$$s(A)\coloneqq \iota^{-1}\Psi (A).$$


Then $s$ is a positive linear map and satisfies $(\pi\otimes 1)\iota s=1$ and $\|s(A)\|=\|A\|$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The map $s$ is positive, linear and contractive because both $\Psi$ and $\iota^{-1}$ have these properties on their respective domains. To verify $(\pi\otimes1)\iota s=1$, it again suffices to consider $*$-monomials $A=\widetilde{V_1}^{*n_1}\widetilde{V_2}^{*n_2}\widetilde{V_1}^{n_3}\widetilde{V_2}^{n_4}$, $n_i\geq 0 $. Using the computation of $\Psi(A)$ above and the properties of the minimal $q$-commuting unitary extension, we get 
\begin{align*}(\pi\otimes 1)\iota s(A)=(\pi\otimes 1)\Psi(A)=A.
\end{align*}
Finally, since $(\pi\otimes1)\iota$ is contractive,
$$\|A\|=\|(\pi\otimes 1)\iota s(A)\|\leq \|s(A)\|\leq \|A\|.
$$
Thus, $s$ is an isometry.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{T:Represent}
Every $X\in C^*(V_1,V_2)$ can be written uniquely as $X=T_A+D$ for some $A\in C^*(\widetilde{V}_1,\widetilde{V}_2)$ and $D\in{\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{T:Fredholm}
If $\pi'$ has a completely positive linear cross section, then for $T_A+D\in C^*(V_1,V_2)$ we have $(\pi\otimes 1)\iota(T_A+D)=A$, and $T_A+D$ is Fredholm if and only if both $A$ and $(1\otimes \pi')\iota(T_A+D)$ are invertible.
In particular, the conclusion holds if $C^*(P,U,{\mathcal K})/{\mathcal K}$ is commutative.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{L:Defect kernel}, the map $(\pi\otimes 1)\iota$ is a $*$-homomorphism and satisfies $(\pi\otimes 1)\iota(D)=0$ for all $D\in {\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$. Moreover, $(\pi\otimes 1)\iota(T_A)=A$ for all $A\in C^*(\widetilde{V}_1,\widetilde{V}_2)$ (see Theorem~\ref{T:Generalized Toeplitz}). Hence $(\pi\otimes 1)\iota(T_A+D)=A$. The Fredholm criterion then follows from the discussion surrounding \eqref{Eq:symbol}.

As noted in the discussion preceding Theorem \ref{T:quotient}, when $C^*(P,U,{\mathcal K})/{\mathcal K}$ is commutative and separable, the quotient map $\pi'$ admits a completely positive cross section.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{D:maximal}
We say that $Y$ is \emph{maximal} if for every $w\in{\mathbb T}$ both $(w,0)$ and $(w,1)$ lie in $Y$, i.e., when $Y$ is the disjoint union of two copies of the unit circle.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{T:semifredimplesfred}
Suppose $(V_1,V_2)$ is a $q$-commuting isometric pair with $({\mathcal F},P,U)$ as its BCL triple such that $C^*(P,U,{\mathcal K})/{\mathcal K}$ is commutative. If $\alpha I+D$ is semi-Fredholm for some $D\in {\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$ and $\alpha\in {\mathbb C}\setminus \{0\}$, then $\alpha I+D$ is Fredholm.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
As discussed earlier, $\alpha I+D$ is semi-Fredholm if and only if $$
\alpha I+(1\otimes \pi')\iota(D)(y)=g(y)$$ is left or right invertible in $\{\mu I+C(Y,K):\mu\in {\mathbb C}\}$ for each $y\in Y$. An application of the classical Fredholm alternative (see e.g., \cite[Theorem 5.22]{MR1634900}) yields the invertibility of $g(y)$ for each $y$. Hence $g$ is invertible, and the conclusion follows.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{L:FredQuotient}
If $(V_1,V_2)$ is essentially doubly $q$-commuting with $({\mathcal F},P,U)$ as the associated BCL triple, then $PUP\vert_{\mathrm{ran}P}$ is Fredholm if and only if $C^*(P,U,{\mathcal K})/{\mathcal K}$ is commutative.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
If $C^*(P,U,{\mathcal K})/{\mathcal K}$ is commutative, then and only then $PU-UP$ is compact. This implies $P^\perp UP$ is compact. Now apply Lemma~\ref{L:block-unitary-index} to the unitary $U$ with respect to the decomposition ${\mathcal F} = \operatorname{ran}P \oplus \operatorname{ran}P^\perp$ to get $PUP|_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ Fredholm. Conversely, if $PUP|_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is Fredholm, then by Lemma \ref{L:block-unitary-index} again, both $P^\perp UP|_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ and $P UP^\perp|_{\operatorname{ran}P^\perp}$ are compact, which is same as $PU-UP$ being compact, or equivalently, the quotient $C^*(P,U,{\mathcal K})/{\mathcal K}$ is commutative.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{T:kappa_pair_invariant}
For an essentially doubly $q$-commuting isometric pair $(V_1,V_2)$, the quantity $\kappa(V_1,V_2)$ is a unitary invariant of the pair.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $(V_1,V_2)$ and $(V_1',V_2')$ be essentially doubly $q$-commuting pairs of isometries on ${\mathcal H}$ and ${\mathcal H}'$, respectively, and let $({\mathcal F},P,U)$ and $({\mathcal F}',P',U')$ be their corresponding BCL triples. By \Cref{T:q-BCL}, the pairs $(V_1,V_2)$ and $(V_1',V_2')$ are unitarily equivalent if and only if the triples $({\mathcal F},P,U)$ and $({\mathcal F}',P',U')$ are unitarily equivalent. This implies $PUP\vert_{\mathrm{ran}P}$ and $P'U'P'\vert_{\mathrm{ran}P'}$ are unitarily equivalent, and hence have the same Fredholm index.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{T:cp_section}
For an essentially doubly $q$-commuting isometric pair $(V_1,V_2)$, the quotient map $\pi'$ admits a completely positive cross section. Moreover, if $\kappa(V_1,V_2)=0$ then $\pi'$ admits a $*$-isomorphic cross section.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $(V_1,V_2)$ be essentially doubly $q$-commuting with BCL triple $({\mathcal F},P,U)$. Then the associated commuting pair $(R_{\overline{q}}V_1, V_2R_{q})$ is essentially doubly commuting with the same BCL triple. By \cite[Theorem 5.3]{MR467392}, the quotient map $\pi'$ admits a completely positive cross section. If, in addition, $\kappa(V_1,V_2)=0$, then \cite[Lemma 7.1]{MR467392} shows that $\pi'$ admits a $*$-isomorphic cross section.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{indformula}
Assume that $\kappa(V_1,V_2)$ is finite and nonzero. Let $Y$, as in the discussion preceding Theorem \ref{T:semifredimplesfred}, be the homeomorphic image of the maximal ideal space of the (commutative) quotient algebra $C^*(P,U,{\mathcal K})/{\mathcal K}$ associated to $(V_1,V_2)$. Then $Y$ is maximal in the sense of Definition \ref{D:maximal}, and every Fredholm operator of the form $I+D$ with $D\in{\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$ satisfies
$$
\operatorname{ind} (I+D)=-\kappa(V_1,V_2)(n_1+n_2),
$$
where $(1\otimes \pi')\iota(I+D)$ is homotopic to $f_1^{n_1}f_2^{n_2}$ for some integers $n_1,n_2$.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The proof that $Y$ is maximal is the same as in \cite[Theorem 6.1]{MR467392}. By the index formula \eqref{Eq:ind(B_1)}, it suffices to show that $\operatorname{ind}(B_1)=-\kappa(V_1,V_2)$, where $B_1$ is the Fredholm operator as in \eqref{B1B2}. With respect to the decomposition $H^2({\mathcal F})={\mathcal F}\oplus (\operatorname{ran}\widetilde{P_0}^\perp\otimes {\mathcal F})$, the operator $B_1$ is the direct sum of $P^\perp U-P$ acting on ${\mathcal F}$ and the identity operator on $\operatorname{ran}\widetilde{P_0}^\perp\otimes {\mathcal F}$. Thus $\operatorname{ind}(B_1)=\operatorname{ind}(P^\perp U-P)$. With respect to the decomposition ${\mathcal F} = \operatorname{ran}P +\operatorname{ran}P^\perp$, we have
\begin{align}\label{Computation}
P^\perp U - P = \begin{bmatrix}
    -I_{\operatorname{ran}P} & 0\\
    0 & P^\perp UP^\perp|_{\operatorname{ran}P^\perp}
\end{bmatrix}  + \begin{bmatrix}
     0 & 0\\
     P^\perp UP|_{\operatorname{ran}P} & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{align}Now $P^\perp UP = UP - PUP = UP - PU + PUP^\perp$. Since $(V_1,V_2)$ is essentially doubly $q$-commuting, $PUP^\perp$ is compact. Since $\kappa(V_1,V_2)$ is finite, by Lemma \ref{L:FredQuotient}, $PU-UP$ is compact, hence $P^\perp UP$ is compact. Since the index is invariant under compact perturbation, by \eqref{Computation}, we have
$$
\operatorname{ind}(B_1) = \operatorname{ind}(P^\perp U -P) = \operatorname{ind}(P^\perp U P^\perp|_{\operatorname{ran}P^\perp} = -\operatorname{ind}(PUP|_{\operatorname{ran}P}) = -\kappa(V_1,V_2),
$$where to obtain the second equality we used Lemma \ref{L:block-unitary-index}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{T:I+D}
For an essentially doubly $q$-commuting isometric pair $(V_1,V_2)$ with infinite dimensional coefficient space, the operator $I+D(V_1,V_2)$ is semi-Fredholm and
$$
\kappa(V_1,V_2)=-\operatorname{ind} (I+D(V_1,V_2))
$$
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
A direct computation gives $I+D(V_1,V_2)=V_2V_2^*+[V_2^*,V_2]V_1[V_2^*,V_2]$. By Theorem \ref{T:CommIdeal}, this operator unitarily equivalent to
\begin{align*}
&I-(\widetilde{P_0}\otimes P^\perp)+ (\widetilde{P_0}\otimes P^\perp)(T_z R_q \otimes UP + R_q\otimes UP^\perp)(\widetilde{P_0}\otimes P^\perp)\\
&= (I-\widetilde{P_0})\otimes I+\widetilde{P_0}\otimes P+ \widetilde{P_0}R_q\widetilde{P_0}\otimes P^\perp UP^\perp=(I-\widetilde{P_0})\otimes I+\widetilde{P_0}\otimes (P+P^\perp UP^\perp),
\end{align*}
where we used $\widetilde{P_0}R_q\widetilde{P_0}=\widetilde{P_0}$. With respect to the decomposition $H^2\otimes {\mathcal F}=\widetilde{P_0}H^2\otimes{\mathcal F}\oplus(I-\widetilde{P_0})H^2\otimes{\mathcal F}={\mathbb C} e_0\otimes{\mathcal F}\oplus(I-\widetilde{P_0})H^2\otimes{\mathcal F}$, we obtain the block diagonal form

$$\iota(I+D(V_1,V_2))=\begin{bmatrix}
P+P^\perp UP^\perp & 0\\
0&I  
\end{bmatrix}.$$
Thus it suffices to show that $P+P^\perp UP^\perp$ is semi-Fredholm on ${\mathcal F}$. Equivalently, the restriction $P^\perp UP^\perp\vert_{\operatorname{ran} P^\perp}$ is semi-Fredholm on $\operatorname{ran} P^\perp$ and $$\operatorname{ind} (P^\perp UP^\perp\mid_{\operatorname{ran} P^\perp})=-\operatorname{ind} PUP\mid_{\textit{ran} P}.$$ Since $PUP^\perp$ is compact, we apply Lemma~\ref{L:block-unitary-index} to the block decomposition of the unitary $$U=\begin{bmatrix}PUP\vert_{\operatorname{ran} P} & PUP^\perp \vert_{\operatorname{ran} P^\perp}\\ P^\perp UP\vert_{\operatorname{ran} P} & P^\perp UP^\perp\vert_{\operatorname{ran} P^\perp}
\end{bmatrix}
$$ and obtain the desired conclusion.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{T:ind(I+D)=0}
If $\kappa(V_1,V_2)=0$ and $D$ in the defect ideal ${\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$ is such that $I+D$ is Fredholm, then $\operatorname{ind}(I+D)=0$.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{T:cp_section}, if $\kappa(V_1,V_2)=0$ then the quotient map $\pi'$ admits a $*$-isomorphic cross section, say $\rho$. By Theorem \ref{T:CommIdeal}, we also have $\iota({\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}})={\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U)$. Suppose that $I+D$ is Fredholm. Then $I+(1\otimes\pi')\iota(D)$ is invertible, and hence so is $I+(1\otimes\rho\pi')\iota(D)$. Since $\iota(D)\in{\mathcal K}\otimes C^*(P,U)$, the difference $(1\otimes\rho\pi')\iota(D)-\iota(D)$ is compact. Therefore $\iota(I+D)$ is a compact perturbation of an invertible operator, and hence is Fredholm of index $0$. Since $\iota$ is unitarily implemented, the same holds for $I+D$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{L:ideal_equality}
Let $(V_1,V_2)$ and $(V_1',V_2')$ be $q$-commuting isometries on ${\mathcal H}$ such that $C^*(V_1,V_2)=C^*(V_1',V_2')$. Then ${\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}={\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}'}$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By symmetry it suffices to show that ${\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}'}\subseteq {\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$. It is enough to prove that $I-V_i'V_i'^*\in {\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$ for $i=1,2$.
Let $\pi\colon C^*(V_1,V_2)\to C^*(V_1,V_2)/{\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$ be the quotient map and set
$B\coloneqq C^*(\pi(V_1),\pi(V_2))$. Since $V_i'\in C^*(V_1,V_2)$ is an isometry, $\pi(V_i')$ is an isometry in $B$. Once we show that $\pi(V_i')$ is unitary in $B$, we obtain $\pi(I-V_i'V_i'^*)=0$, and hence $I-V_i'V_i'^*\in\ker\pi={\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$.

Recall the discussion preceding Lemma \ref{L:SEirrational}. Since $(\pi(V_1),\pi(V_2))$ is a $q$-commuting unitary pair, the algebra $B$ is canonically isomorphic to the irrational rotation algebra ${\mathcal A}_{\theta}$. Moreover, since ${\mathcal A}_\theta$ admits a (unique) faithful trace, every isometry in ${\mathcal A}_{\theta}$ is unitary. Indeed, if $v\in{\mathcal A}_{\theta}$ is an isometry and $\tau$ denotes the faithful trace, then  $$\tau(1-vv^*)=\tau(1)-\tau(vv^*)=\tau(1)-\tau(v^*v)=0.$$ By faithfulness of $\tau$, we conclude $vv^*=1$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{T:kappa_Cstar_invariant}
Let $(V_1,V_2)$ be a pair of $q$-commuting isometries such that $V_2^*V_1-qV_1V_2^*$ is compact. Then $|\kappa(V_1,V_2)|$ is a unitary invariant for $C^*(V_1,V_2)$.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $\tau\colon {\mathcal H}\to {\mathcal H}'$ be a unitary such that $\tau C^*(V_1,V_2)\tau^*=C^*(V_1',V_2')$ and $(V_1'',V_2'')\coloneqq \tau^*(V_1',V_2')\tau$.
Then $(V_1'',V_2'')$ is essentially doubly $q$-commuting and $C^*(V_1,V_2)=C^*(V_1'',V_2'').$
Since $(V_1'',V_2'')$ is unitarily equivalent to $(V_1',V_2')$, Theorem~\ref{T:kappa_pair_invariant} gives $\kappa(V_1',V_2')=\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')$. Hence it suffices to prove that $|\kappa(V_1,V_2)|=|\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')|$.
We consider three cases, according to the value of $\kappa(V_1,V_2)$.


\textbf{Case I:} Assume $\kappa(V_1,V_2)=0$. By \Cref{T:I+D} applied to $(V_1'',V_2'')$, the operator $I+D(V_1'',V_2'')$ is semi-Fredholm of index $-\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')$. Since ${\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}={\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}''}$, we may view  $I+D(V_1'',V_2'')$ as an element of $ C^*(V_1,V_2)$ of the form $I+D$ with $D\in {\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}}$. Since $(V_1,V_2)$ is essentially doubly $q$-commuting, by Lemma \ref{L:FredQuotient} and the discussion preceding it,  $\kappa(V_1,V_2)=0$ implies $C^*(P,U,{\mathcal K})/{\mathcal K}$ is commutative. By \Cref{T:semifredimplesfred}, $I+D(V_1'',V_2'')=I+D$ is in fact Fredholm. Then by \Cref{T:ind(I+D)=0}, 
$$
0=\operatorname{ind}(I+D)=\operatorname{ind} (I+D(V_1'',V_2''))=\kappa (V_1'',V_2'')
$$ and hence $\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')=0$ as was required to show.

Let us note in addition that the argument above can be reversed to show $\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')=0$ implies $\kappa(V_1,V_2)=0$. For this direction, one needs to work with the semi-Fredholm element $I+D(V_1,V_2)$ instead follow the same line of arguments as given above.

\textbf{Case II:} Assume $0<|\kappa(V_1,V_2)|<\infty$. As observed in Case~I, we may rule out the possibility $\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')=0$. Since ${\mathcal I}_{\mathcal D}={\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}''}$, we can view $I+D(V_1'',V_2'')$ as an element of $C^*(V_1,V_2)$. By the assumption that $\kappa(V_1,V_2)<\infty$, the associated quotient $C^*(P,U,{\mathcal K})/{\mathcal K}$ is commutative (by Lemma \ref{L:FredQuotient}). This makes Theorem \ref{T:semifredimplesfred} applicable to the pair $(V_1,V_2)$, which implies that $I+D(V_1'',V_2'')$, viewed as an element of $C^*(V_1,V_2)$, is Fredholm. By \Cref{T:I+D} applied to $(V_1'',V_2'')$, 
$$
\kappa(V_1'',V_2'') =  - \operatorname{ind}(I+D(V_1'',V_2'')) <\infty.
$$

Thus $\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')$ can neither be zero nor infinite. It remains to show that $|\kappa(V_1,V_2)|=|\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')|$. Since $k(V_1'',V_2'')$ is nonzero and finite, we apply Theorem \ref{indformula} for the pair $(V_1'',V_2'')$ and the element $D(V_1,V_2)\in {\mathcal I}_{\mathcal D}={\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}''}$ to get an integer $N''$ such that
\begin{align}\label{Aux'}
N''\cdot \kappa(V_1'',V_2'') = \operatorname{ind}(I+D(V_1,V_2))=\kappa(V_1,V_2),
\end{align}where to obtain the last equality we applied Theorem \ref{T:I+D} to $(V_1,V_2)$. Since $k(V_1,V_2)$ is also nonzero and finite, Theorem \ref{indformula} can also be applied to $(V_1,V_2)$ for the element $D(V_1'',V_2'')\in {\mathcal I}_{{\mathcal D}''}={\mathcal I}_{\mathcal D}$ to get an integer $N$ so that
\begin{align}\label{Aux''}
N\cdot \kappa(V_1,V_2) = \operatorname{ind}(I+D(V_1'',V_2''))=\kappa(V_1'',V_2''),
\end{align}where, as before, to obtain the last equality we applied Theorem \ref{T:I+D} to $(V_1'',V_2'')$. Equations \eqref{Aux'} and \eqref{Aux''} imply that $\kappa(V_1,V_2)$ and $\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')$ divides each other, hence $|\kappa(V_1,V_2)|=|\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')|$.

Finally, the set of arguments above can be reversed to obtain the reverse implication: 
$$
0<|\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')|<\infty\:\Longrightarrow 0<|\kappa(V_1,V_2)|<\infty.
$$

\textbf{Case III:} Assume $\kappa(V_1,V_2)=\infty$. The possibilities $\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')=0$ and $0<|\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')|<\infty$ are ruled out by the previous arguments in Cases I and II. Hence $\kappa(V_1'',V_2'')=\infty$ as well.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
